Packing for a Week-Long Motorcycle Tour

Seven days on a motorcycle through Britain. It's enough time to ride from the Channel Islands to Cape Wrath, explore the entirety of Wales, or loop the Scottish Highlands at a civilised pace. But a week demands more careful packing than an overnighter. Here's everything you need — and nothing you don't.

Luggage Setup

For a week's touring, you'll want a proper luggage system. Options include:

  • Panniers (hard or soft): 30-40L per side gives ample space. Hard panniers offer security and weather protection; soft panniers are lighter and more forgiving on narrow lanes.
  • Tail bag: 20-40L on the pillion seat for overflow and easy-access items.
  • Tank bag: 5-15L for daily essentials, phone, wallet, snacks. Magnetic or strap-mounted depending on your tank material.

Total capacity of 80-100 litres is the sweet spot for a week's kit with a mix of camping and accommodation nights.

Clothing Strategy

The trick is to pack three days' worth and wash mid-tour. Most B&Bs will let you hang things to dry, and launderettes exist in most market towns.

  • 3 sets of underwear and socks (merino wool dries fast and doesn't smell quickly)
  • 3 t-shirts or base layers
  • 2 pairs of casual trousers or shorts
  • 1 warm mid-layer (fleece or lightweight down jacket)
  • 1 pair of lightweight shoes for off-bike
  • Swimwear
  • 1 smart-casual outfit if you plan any nicer dinners

Riding Gear for a Full Week

Your riding kit takes the most abuse over a week. Plan accordingly:

  • Jacket and trousers: A quality textile touring suit with removable thermal and waterproof liners is the most versatile option for UK conditions.
  • Two pairs of gloves: Summer and waterproof. Rotate and dry them out.
  • Waterproof over-suit: Even with waterproof textiles, a dedicated over-suit for truly awful days is worth the space.
  • Heated gear: If touring outside June-August, heated grips or a heated vest make cold mornings bearable.
  • Spare visor: A clear visor for night riding and a tinted or transition visor for daytime is ideal.
  • Neck tubes (x2): Lightweight, packable, incredibly useful for temperature regulation.

Tools and Spares

  • Full tool roll matching your bike's fasteners
  • Tyre repair kit with plugs and CO2 cartridges
  • Chain lube and a rag
  • Spare clutch and brake levers (if your bike uses exposed levers)
  • Spare bulbs
  • Cable ties, gaffer tape, wire
  • Small bottle of engine oil (for top-ups)
  • Tyre pressure gauge

Camping Additions

If you're mixing in camping nights to save money and add adventure:

  • Lightweight 2-person tent (more room for gear inside)
  • Sleeping bag rated to 5°C minimum (UK summer nights can be cold)
  • Self-inflating sleeping mat
  • Compact stove, pot, and lighter
  • Microfibre towel
  • Head torch with spare batteries
Weight distribution matters more over a week than a weekend. Repack and redistribute every couple of days as you consume supplies and your kit settles. Heavy items always go low and close to the bike's centre.

Electronics

  • Phone with offline maps
  • USB power bank (20,000mAh recommended for a week)
  • Charging cables for all devices
  • 12V USB socket on the bike (install before departure if you don't have one)
  • Camera and memory cards
  • Bluetooth intercom system (charged nightly)

Comfort and Wellbeing

  • Earplugs (essential for long days in the saddle — wind noise causes fatigue)
  • Sunscreen and lip balm
  • Insect repellent (vital in Scotland June-September)
  • Any regular medication plus basic painkillers
  • A good book or Kindle for rainy rest days

Pack it all, do a test load on the bike, ride around the block, and adjust. The hour you spend optimising your load before departure will pay dividends every single day of your week on the road.
keyTakeaways: Aim for 80-100 litres of luggage for a week mixing camping and accommodation nights.
Pack three days of clothing and wash mid-tour; merino wool dries fast and resists odour.
A textile touring suit with removable thermal and waterproof liners is the most versatile UK setup.
Carry a 20,000mAh power bank for a week and fit a 12V USB socket before departure.
Repack and redistribute weight every couple of days, keeping heavy items low and central.

faq.q: How much luggage capacity do I need for a week?
faq.a: Around 80 to 100 litres is the sweet spot for a week's kit with a mix of camping and accommodation nights. A pannier pair of 30 to 40 litres per side, a 20 to 40 litre tail bag and a 5 to 15 litre tank bag covers it. Hard panniers add security and weather protection, while soft panniers are lighter and better on narrow lanes.

faq.q: How do I handle clothing for seven days?
faq.a: Pack three days' worth and wash mid-tour. Most B&Bs let you hang things to dry and launderettes exist in most market towns. Bring three sets of merino underwear and socks, which dry fast and do not smell quickly, three base layers, two pairs of casual trousers, one warm mid-layer and one pair of off-bike shoes.

faq.q: What riding gear suits a full UK week?
faq.a: A quality textile touring suit with removable thermal and waterproof liners is the most versatile option for changeable UK conditions. Add two pairs of gloves (summer and waterproof) to rotate and dry, a dedicated waterproof over-suit for truly awful days, a spare clear visor for night riding, and heated gear if you are touring outside June to August.

Carry your phone with offline maps, a 20,000mAh power bank for a week, charging cables for every device, a camera with spare memory cards and a Bluetooth intercom charged nightly. Fit a 12V USB socket to the bike before departure if you do not already have one, so you can charge on the move.

faq.q: How often should I repack on a long tour?
faq.a: Repack and redistribute weight every couple of days as you consume supplies and your kit settles. Weight distribution matters more over a week than a weekend, so always keep heavy items low and close to the bike's centre. Do a test load, ride around the block and adjust before you leave.
